candidate_answers.answer: Use a hash map to store each previously seen value and its index. For each number, calculate target minus that number and check whether the complement is already in the map. If it is, return the stored index and current index. Otherwise, store the current number and index. This takes O(n) time and O(n) space.
Use a hash map to find the complement of each number and return the matching indices.
Use two nested loops to examine every pair of elements. If the two values add up to the target, return their indices. This takes O(n^2) time and O(1) additional space.

I would use a stack. Push opening brackets. For a closing bracket, the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opening bracket; otherwise return false. At the end the stack must be empty. This is O(n) time and O(n) space. Empty input and mismatched or early closing brackets are handled.

Because the array is sorted, I would keep left and right pointers and repeatedly check the middle. If nums[mid] is too small I move left to mid+1; if too large I move right to mid-1; otherwise I return mid. This is O(log n) time and O(1) space. Empty arrays and absent targets are handled.

I would use binary search with left, right, and mid. If the middle is too small move left, otherwise move right. I would return the index when found. I haven't considered an empty array or the exact behavior when the target is absent.

I would sort the intervals by start time. Then keep the last merged interval and compare each new interval's start with its end. If they overlap, extend the end; otherwise append a new interval. Sorting dominates at O(n log n), and the merge pass is O(n). I would handle empty input and touching/overlapping boundaries consistently.
I would compare every interval against the others and repeatedly merge overlaps until no more merges are possible. This can work, but sorting once and doing a single pass is more efficient.

I would sort by start time and merge intervals in one pass. The logic is correct. I think the overall time is O(n) because after sorting we only traverse once, and sorting does not change the overall linear behavior.

I would sort intervals by their starting values and merge whenever the next start is less than the current end. I haven't considered whether touching intervals should merge, empty input, or intervals contained completely inside another interval.
I would compare each interval with the next interval and merge them if they overlap. I don't think sorting is necessary because the input already represents intervals that are close together.

I would use Kadane's algorithm. Maintain the best subarray ending at the current position and the global best. At each element choose between starting a new subarray or extending the current one. This is O(n) time and O(1) extra space. I would initialize from the first element so an all-negative array is handled correctly.

I would check every possible subarray and calculate its sum, keeping the maximum. This is correct but much slower than Kadane's algorithm and can be O(n^2) or O(n^3) depending on how sums are computed.

I would maintain a current sum and maximum sum, adding each value and resetting when the current sum becomes negative. The approach is Kadane's algorithm. I think it is O(n^2) because the maximum is updated repeatedly, with O(1) space.
